sections.h2: What shapes the housing market in Lanier County?
sections.html:
Lanier County is a small south Georgia county made from parts of Berrien, Clinch and Lowndes counties in 1920, making it the state's 157th. Lakeland is the county seat, and the town's old name was Milltown until it incorporated in 1925 and took a name that points to the lakes around it. Banks Lake, Grand Bay Lake and Lake Irma are all in the county, and Banks Lake National Wildlife Refuge, established in 1985, covers more than 4,000 acres of water, marsh and swamp.

The New Georgia Encyclopedia lists Moody Air Force Base, which Lanier shares with Lowndes County, the hospital, the lakes and a large state correctional facility among the factors behind the local economy. Stockton, once called Registerville, is the other named community. Fishing on the lakes and the Alapaha River has long been part of the county's identity, and the courthouse, replaced in 1973, sits in Lakeland, where downtown buildings carry murals of 1920s community life.

sections.h2: What do Census figures show for Lanier County?
sections.html:
Lanier County added 7.6% to its population between the 2020 estimates base and July 2025, which is much faster than Jones or Johnson County.

Persons per household average 2.82, the largest of the four counties, and 8.0% of residents age five and up speak a language other than English at home. The 73.2% ownership rate is the lowest in the group, so a rental house is a realistic thing to sell here. Thirty-nine permits in 2025 is a small number, so a listing competes mostly with other resale homes.

sections.h2: Who handles property tax in Lanier County?
sections.html:
All three county offices that matter to a seller are in the same stretch of West Main Street in Lakeland, GA 31635.

  • Tax Commissioner: 56 W Main St, Suite 1, (229) 482-3795, open Monday through Friday 8:00 a.m. to noon and 1:00 p.m. to 5:00 p.m. The commissioner collects property tax and acts as the state's tag agent for motor vehicles.
  • Tax Assessor: 56 W Main Street, Suite 2, (229) 482-2090, open 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., with parcel records on qPublic.
  • Board of Commissioners: Suite 9, (229) 482-2088.
  • Probate and Superior Court: (229) 482-3668 and (229) 482-3594, per the county's contact list.

Online payment is available through the county's GovtWindow page. Office details are posted at laniercountyboc.com, and parcel lookups run through the assessor's qPublic link.

sections.h2: What is the Lanier County property tax due date?
sections.html:
The state default is December 20, and the Georgia Department of Revenue says a local governing authority may change it to December 1 or November 15, or bill in installments. Lanier County's own site does not print a date, so call the tax commissioner at (229) 482-3795 and ask which one your bill uses.

Every taxpayer gets 60 days from the postmark of the bill before interest accrues, and unpaid balances can later carry penalties. The Revenue Department's FAQ says a property owner on January 1 owes the full year's tax even after a quick sale, with no refund for part-year ownership. County liens go on file with the Clerk of Superior Court, where a title examiner will look when your house goes under contract.

Mobile homes follow a separate calendar. A home placed in the county needs a location permit within 30 days, and the permit renews between January 1 and April 1. The owner on January 1 must also return the mobile home to the tax commissioner by April 1.

sections.h2: Does Lanier County offer homestead exemptions?
sections.html:
The Revenue Department's county page says Lanier County has no local homestead exemptions. Owners can still apply for the statewide homestead exemptions, plus the disabled veterans exemption, which the page says applies to city and county taxes.

  • Apply with the county tax office at any time once the property is your primary residence.
  • The application must be received by April 1 of the first year you want the exemption.
  • Not applying is treated as a waiver for that year.
  • Commercial and industrial inventory can be exempt if county voters approved a freeport exemption, which is requested through the assessors.

Before asking about a break, find out whether the seller has already filed. Georgia counties renew an exemption automatically only until ownership or residence changes, so a buyer who moves in files a new application by April 1 of the first tax year. If you are the seller, ask the commissioner whether your exemption was active for the year so the closing figures reflect it.

sections.h2: How do I appeal a Lanier County assessment?
sections.html:
The Board of Tax Assessors mails an annual notice for real property, and the owner has 45 days from the mailing date to appeal the fair market value. The appeal is in writing and goes first to the board of tax assessors. The Revenue Department says the board may accept it by email if the county has adopted a written policy consenting to electronic service.

The owner picks one of three routes: the county Board of Equalization, a hearing officer or an arbitrator. The state supplies a uniform appeal form, and grounds can be taxability, value, uniformity or the denial of an exemption. The Revenue Department cannot override the assessors, the board, the hearing officer, the arbitrator or Superior Court on an individual appraisal.

Georgia does not set a revaluation schedule. Each county reviews values against sales every year and adjusts where they fall short or run high, so a notice can arrive in any year.

sections.h2: How can I sell a Lanier County property that has back taxes?
sections.html:
Request a payoff from the tax commissioner and ask whether any lien has been recorded. A closing attorney or title company can wire the payoff before releasing proceeds. Georgia also requires the holder of a long-term note secured by real estate to record the security instrument in the county within 90 days, and the Revenue Department prints the recording tax at $1.50 for each $500 or fractional part of the note's face amount. In most counties the Clerk of Superior Court collects it.

Heirs selling a house should ask Lanier County Probate about opening the estate first. A buyer purchasing for cash from a family that lives out of town can usually work with a tax payoff taken from the sale price at the closing table.

faqs.q: Where is the Lanier County Tax Commissioner's office?
faqs.a: At 56 W Main St, Suite 1, Lakeland, GA 31635. The phone is (229) 482-3795 and the office is open Monday through Friday from 8:00 a.m. to noon and 1:00 p.m. to 5:00 p.m.

faqs.q: When are property taxes due in Lanier County?
faqs.a: Georgia's default is December 20, but a county can choose December 1, November 15 or installments. Call (229) 482-3795 for the date on your bill. Interest does not begin until 60 days after the bill's postmark.

faqs.q: Are there local homestead exemptions in Lanier County?
faqs.a: No. The Georgia Department of Revenue's county fact sheet says none are offered locally. You can apply for the statewide homestead exemptions and the disabled veterans exemption by April 1.

faqs.q: What is the median home value in Lanier County?
faqs.a: The Census Bureau lists $162,300 for owner-occupied homes in 2020-2024. Median gross rent is $913 and the owner-occupied rate is 73.2%.

faqs.q: Can I appeal by email in Lanier County?
faqs.a: Only if the board of tax assessors has adopted a written policy consenting to electronic service. Otherwise mail the written appeal within 45 days of the notice mailing date. Call the assessor at (229) 482-2090 to ask.
